event.title: Bank of America Museums on Us
event.description:
Bank of America cardholders receive free general admission – during the first full weekend of every month – to cultural institutions across the United States.

How to visit:
Present your active Bank of America, Merrill or Bank of America Private Bank credit or debit card and valid government issued photo ID (Passport booklet, State ID, Driver License) to receive one free general admission to either museum location.

Please review eligibility and terms prior to your visit:

  • Museums on Us is available to Bank of America, Merrill, or Bank of America Private Bank credit and debit cardholders during the first full weekend of every month.
  • The offer is valid for one general admission only per eligible cardholder.
  • Any special exhibitions, ticketed exhibitions, enhanced experiences, or additional offerings are not included and must be purchased separately.
  • This offer is limited to the individual cardholder, is not transferable, does not guarantee admission, and cannot be combined with other offers.
  • Fundraising events are excluded.

event.description:
As America’s premier John Denver tribute artist, Ted Vigil has wowed sellout crowds from coast to coast. He embodies the late great music icon in look as well as voice with an unforgettable performance. He was invited to perform as the John Denver tribute artist at John Denver’s “Windstar Foundation” in Aspen, Colorado. John Denver’s lead guitarist, Steve Weisberg, performed with Ted and described his performance as “uncanny”.

For this wonderful and exciting performance, expect to hear John Denver’s most beloved hits, like ‘Take Me Home Country Roads”, “Leaving on a Jet Plane”, “Annie’s Song”. “Rocky Mountain High”, “Sunshine On My Shoulder”, ‘Thank God I’m a Country Boy” and many more. If you are A John Denver fan you definitely will not want to miss this performance.

There are a limited number of VIP 1 seats available to this event. They include best in house seating in the first three rows, meet & greet with the artist and a photo opportunity. Also, includes a free glass of wine and a fantastic piece of cheesecake from Indulge Artisan Cheesecake in Medford.

Gary Gulman “Grandiloquent”

Acclaimed comedian and author Gary Gulman brings his hilarious new show Grandiloquent to the Craterian stage. This 80-minute, whip-smart and unexpectedly moving performance showcases Gulman’s signature blend of clever wit and emotional honesty. Drawing from his childhood, love of literature, and personal insecurities, Grandiloquent explores themes of empathy, self-acceptance, and the coping power of humor, reading, and writing. Known for acclaimed specials like Born on 3rd Base and The Great Depresh, Gulman continues to prove why he’s one of the most compelling voices in comedy today.

Get ready for a swingin’ night of timeless music as the legendary Tommy Dorsey Orchestra showcases its iconic big-band sound in a dazzling tribute to Frank Sinatra. Featuring vocalist Hayden Grove (from Season 27 of The Voice), this electrifying performance celebrates Sinatra’s early years with the Dorsey Orchestra in the 1940s—the era that launched his rise to superstardom. With unforgettable classics, soaring brass, and the energy of one of the greatest dance bands of all time, this full-swing celebration captures the rhythm, romance, and excitement that made the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra a legend.

event.description:

Rocky Horror Picture Show Original Cast Spooktacular

“Costume Contest!” Come in costume for a chance to win a prize!”

Join Patricia Quinn (the original “Magenta”) for a screening of the 1975 cult-classic, The Rocky Horror Picture Show, complete with a live shadow cast and audience participation! Celebrated for its campy, outrageous style and inclusive, gender-bending themes, Rocky Horror follows newlyweds Brad and Janet, who stumble into the castle of the mad-scientist alien, Dr. Frank-N-Furter—where their innocence quickly unravels. The longest-running theatrical release in history, it’s a deliciously bizarre cult phenomenon that practically begs for audience participation.

Live screenings are highly interactive (some might even say raucous!), and this R-rated film features mature themes not appropriate for all audiences.

VIP UPGRADE!

Limited to 100 participant.

The upgrade will include a premium section A VIP 1 seat, meet & greet with Patricia Quinn, VIP Lanyard, photo opportunity and a signed photo (or one personal item).

You will get an email with VIP location and start time a week before the show.

The Rocky Horror Experience

* The Rocky Horror Tour & The Craterian Theater want to make sure that everyone has a great time at the RHPS.

The idea behind Rocky Horror’s traditions—shouting callback lines, throwing props, and dressing up is to have FUN, not to be destructive to the venue or disruptive to fellow fans. Every venue and every Rocky Horror experience is unique. The following guidelines will help you and other members of the audience enjoy this special night at the Craterian. Please ensure that you are conscious of those around you and respectful of theater staff and volunteers. 

  • You CAN use props, but only when indicated during the show.
  • You CAN purchase a prop bag in the theater lobby prior to the show ($5). No additional props (beyond what is in the bag provided by the Rocky Horror Tour) are allowed into the theater. 
  • You CAN yell, but remember everyone wants to hear and see the movie, so please keep yelling to the appropriate moments.

event.description:
Youth Symphony of Southern Oregon
Fall Concert Series Performance
November 14, 2026, 7:30 p.m.

The Youth Symphony of Southern Oregon (YSSO) will present a performance at the Collier Center’s Craterian Theater at 7:30PM on Saturday, November 14, 2026. The concert will showcase the musicians of the Youth Symphony and the Youth Orchestra under the direction of interim conductor Steve Kessler.

The featured Youth Symphony work on the Fall Concert Series program will be the Finale of Max Bruch’s Violin Concerto No. 1 in G minor, Op. 26. The violin soloist will be 2026 Concerto Competition winner Louvencia Blumhardt. The concert will also include music by Antonin Dvořák, Brian Balmages, Paul Dukas, Nicolai Rimsky-Korsakov, and others.

Since 1988, the Youth Symphony of Southern Oregon has brought accomplished young musicians to the Craterian Theater and stages across the Rogue Valley, performing orchestral masterworks, concerti, film, ballet, and opera scores, and contemporary music. YSSO performances are accessible, audiences are multigenerational, and the impact of the inspiring performances is lasting.

The YSSO believes music is a catalyst for community engagement, personal growth, and a cohesive society. The YSSO supplements school music programs, strengthens the region’s arts sector, and gives young people a place where their contribution genuinely matters. In addition to the performances, the musicians build listening skills, empathy, lasting friendships, and the discipline that comes from mastering intellectual and technical challenges. Whether a YSSO musician goes on to become an engineer, educator, nurse, physician, business or faith leader, parent, professional
musician, attorney, accountant, or astronaut, the habits of collaboration travel with them.

The Youth Symphony of Southern Oregon is an organization in which every person’s sound contributes to the music.

event.title: Oil Painting Simplified With Paul Gallo
event.description:
Weekend workshop: Oct 31, Nov 1

9-4pm

Topics covered:

• Painting Demonstration – 4 oil painting guidelines
• Simplifying with parent colors
• Color mixing
• Big brush advantage
• Straightforward compositions
• Importances of Edges
• Creating depth in your painting

Oil Painting – Paul Gallo 717-608-7190

Supplies can be bought locally at Michaels or on-line at Dick Blick or Cheap Joes.

 

BASIC OIL PAINT COLORS: Ultramarine Blue, Cadmium Yellow Medium, Cadmium Red, Alizarin Crimson Permanent, Burnt Sienna and Titanium White

 

PAINT BRANDS: 

Recommended Professional Brands: Windsor Newton or Gamblin  

Less Expensive Recommended Brands: Gamblin 1980, WindsorNewton “Winton”, or Utrecht

Michaels, Dick Blick and Cheap Joes usually have 9-color paint sets for about $45 which will work fine.

I don’t recommend using the cheapest student grade paints.

 

PAPER TOWELS – 1 roll of paper towels

BRUSHES:

event.title: Min Jin Lee in conversation with Mitchell S. Jackson
event.description:
Literary Arts and The Reser are thrilled to present Min Jin Lee, author of the beloved novels Pachinko (an international bestseller and National Book Award finalist) and Free Food for Millionaires, for a conversation about her new book, American Hagwon.  

 American Hagwon is both “a classic in the making and a novel distinctly of our moment, one that helps us find firmer ground in a world unmoored from a most basic concern: how do we care for one another?” 

Min Jin Lee will be joined in conversation by Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and author Mitchell S. Jackson.

About the book:

In schools and churches, hotel rooms and nail salons, law firms and fried-fish shops; in cramped, dingy apartments and luxury, gated communities, the men, women, and children in American Hagwon struggle to find satisfaction and meaning in a world that seems to grow less forgiving with each passing year. Once comfortably middle class in Korea, John and Helen Koh and their three children—Bo, DH, and Mido—find their lives upended, first by a shocking betrayal by John’s oldest friend, then by the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

Desperately striving to regain their footing, they leave Seoul for Sydney and eventually settle in Southern California—where new vistas of opportunity open up for the children as their parents, strangers in a strange land, must adjust to a new life in which their experience and education mean little, and they set their sights on whatever it takes to provide for their children’s futures. The Kohs, their friends, relatives, and even their foes move in and out of each other’s lives as they navigate new courses across the years, always nursing the almost all-consuming faith that education will lead the next generation to success and security.

In American Hagwon, Min Jin Lee has crafted an unforgettable, panoramic novel where the smallest of gestures can have enormous repercussions, where the bonds of family and of memory twist and fray but rarely break, and where willful self-sacrifice—for the benefit of loved ones and even strangers—is a kind of prayer.

event.title: Andrew Barton, Ali Francis, and Lola Milholland in conversation
event.description:
Literary Arts is excited to welcome author and journalist Ali Francis to celebrate her debut book, The Curious Lives of Vegetables, a wild journey through the hidden histories of plants.

Francis will be joined by Portland writers Lola Milholland (Group Living and Other Recipes) and Andrew Barton (Free Food: earth eating, The Long Loaf, The Myrtlewood Cookbook) for a conversation moderated by environmental journalist and author Devon Fredericksen (How to Camp in the Woods).

Together, they’ll explore what food can tell us about how we live: our relationships with plants and place, the ways knowledge and traditions move between people, what gets lost when food systems become less diverse, and what we might recover by paying closer attention to the things we eat. Moving from vegetables and biodiversity to bread, communal tables, regional foodways, and the everyday work of feeding people, the conversation will consider food not simply as something we consume, but as a reflection of our relationships with the natural world.

About the book:

Why are some carrots purple? What does a 1,000-year-old lotus seed have to tell us about survival? How did a tomato named for Paul Robeson become a political symbol? And what disappears when a vegetable disappears?

In The Curious Lives of Vegetables, Australian journalist Ali Francis goes digging into the astonishing stories hiding in our crisper drawers, gardens, markets, and seed banks. Across more than 100 beautifully illustrated stories, she traces the plants we eat through migration and colonialism, politics and religion, extinction and revival, revealing vegetables as living records of human history — and essential seeds for a more resilient future. 

Along the way, Francis encounters ancient seeds brought back from the dead, vegetables carried across borders by displaced communities, plants transformed by centuries of human preference, and varieties now teetering on the edge of extinction. At once playful, deeply researched, and urgent, The Curious Lives of Vegetables asks us to look again at the ordinary plants on our plates, and to consider their extraordinary importance.

The Literary Arts Bookstore & Cafe is excited to welcome author Kelly Grace Thomas to celebrate the release of her memoir-in-verse, Future Tense. Thomas will be joined in conversation by local poet Joy Sullivan.

About the book:

Reckoning with infertility, adoption, and love under pressure, Kelly Grace Thomas’s Future Tense is a searing memoir-in-verse about a woman’s fight to become a mother while losing her own. 

Thomas spends three years trying for a child who never arrives. As she struggles with infertility, her mother is dying of Stage IV uterine cancer, and the desire for a child turns urgent—a countdown. As her mother’s health deteriorates, time narrows, pressure builds, and the clock refuses to slow. As her marriage strains and the world remakes itself without her, Thomas refuses to give up. The fertility clinic is the coldest place on earth; still, she keeps going—through years of medical gaslighting, IVF consults, mounting debt, and backhanded blame—finally welcoming her daughter through adoption just months before her mother’s death.

Intimate and unflinching, Future Tense interrogates the intertwined joys and griefs of womanhood and motherhood—and how biology can sometimes turn against us. Thomas approaches illness and loss with clarity and care, writing with a generosity that welcomes readers in. Despite their brevity, these poems refuse despair, finding meaning and connection even in the hardest seasons of life.

event.title: Nathaniel Hawthorne: Twice-Told Tales
event.description:
When Henry James came to write his short classic book on his predecessor Nathaniel Hawthorne (who was an important influence on James), he wrote, with tongue in cheek, a description of the cultural and social wasteland that an ambitious American writer faced in Hawthorne’s day in finding material for fiction:

No sovereign, no court,…no aristocracy, no church,…no army, no diplomatic service, no country gentlemen, no palaces, no castles, nor manors, nor old country-houses, nor parsonages, nor thatched cottages nor ivied ruins; no cathedrals, nor abbeys, nor little Norman churches; no great Universities nor public schools; no literature, no novels, no museums, no pictures, no political society, no sporting class…. Some such list as that might be drawn up of the absent things in American life, the effect of which,…upon an English or a French imagination, would probably as a general thing be appalling.

And yet Hawthorne, as James well knew, in his most memorable works created a brilliant array of imaginative fictions drawn from the riches of New England life—its legends, tall tales, landscapes, and history. Rather than being appalled, Hawthorne, as James well knew, in his most memorable works created a brilliant array of imaginative fictions drawn from the riches of New England life—its legends, tall tales, landscapes, and history

This Delve seminar will focus on Hawthorne’s short stories—among the most thrilling, strange, and memorable in the American canon. We will explore his first collection of stories, Twice-Told Tales (1837, 1851) as well as a small selection of extraordinary later stories.

Hawthorne worked his American materials in a diverse range of genres—horror, the gothic, romance, the fantastic, moral tales, allegory—and narrative subjects—ambiguities of love and loss, gender and sex, guilt, conflicts between authority and non-conformists, secrets, science and magic, modernity and tradition, past and present, shadows, and a repudiation of tyranny.

What marks all the works we will delve into during this seminar is mystery, ambiguity, thrills and chills, and a keen sense of the ways in which power seeks to dominate the individual. These characteristics alone make him our contemporary.

Writer and Hawthorne fan Rosemary Mahoney writes:

Whatever form they take, Twice-Told Tales, like salt and sugar on daily staples, are a kind of splendid seasoning, coaxing into acuteness the full, strange flavor of life…. Sit this evening by your brownest lamp and read these stories. If you find yourself unstirred, unengaged, un-creeped, then perhaps—and I propose this in the politest way possible—you should check your pulse.

Texts:
We will use the Modern Library Classics edition of Twice-Told Tales, with an introduction by Mahoney, plus a few stories from his other collections of short stories to be supplied in pdf. These will include the proto-feminist male-gaze horror story “The Birthmark.”

event.title: Nature Writing
event.description:
Throughout this six week course, students will look at the many ways in which humans are connected to our natural surroundings, both urban and remote. Weather, soil, plants, wildlife, changing systems, and more will all be explored. By delving into the inherent close relationship humans have with our natural world, each student’s path to writing their own stories using the natural world as scaffolding will emerge.

Each lesson will be designed to unlock the storyteller within by encouraging observation, reading, and learning about natural systems. Participants will read various forms of nature prose and poetry including work by Mary Oliver, Robin Wall Kimmerer, Barbara Kingsolver, Merlin Sheldrake, Richard Powers, Robert Macfarlane, and more. These readings and the resulting discussions will then serve as a springboard to developing personal tone and style.

Through guided in-class exercises students will work to develop their own narrative voice. Each step in the course will hone in on students’ unique narrative perspectives that reflects their own personal connections to the natural world.

The in-class writing prompts will often draw on lived experiences and are intended to help students find their voice. Whether it’s remembering a favorite hike, gardening in their own backyard, watching a bird from their apartment window, cloud watching, traveling further afield into the wilderness, swimming, or walking a creek path, students will have opportunities to use memory to capture the feeling of decompressing in nature in words. Students will explore various forms and literary devices and styles in the process. Students will then have the opportunity to share these free-writes in class to get feedback from peers and the instructor.

By reading the greats and engaging with the natural world from a personal standpoint, students will develop their understanding of ecology and our human connection to it as a species. By the end of the course, acknowledging human interconnectivity with nature may very well become an inherent part of students’ writing process.

This course invites students to dig deep, observe the world around them, slow down, bask in the beauty of the PNW, and discover how their own unique stories can spring from nature.

event.title: Michael Lewis in conversation with David Shipley
event.description:
Literary Arts is pleased to present #1 New York Times bestselling author and host of Apple’s #1 rated podcast Against the Rules, Michael Lewis, in conversation with The New York Times editor-at-large David Shipley, about his new book, Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State.

If you’re a high school educator interested in bringing students to this event, please contact our Director of Youth Programs at olivia@literary-arts.org

 

About the book: 

In Blockers, Lewis views the “meteor strike” of the second Trump administration through the eyes of the public servants targeted by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). As he says, “Every now and then the world hands you the material for a wild story. The collision between the Trump administration and the civil service is one of those moments. “I’ve had so much fun writing this book that at times it has been hard to know whether to laugh or cry.”  

As Lewis explains, in the new Washington, being a Blocker was the worst thing you could be—especially if you worked in the federal government and wanted to keep your job. A Blocker was a holdover, an impediment, someone who didn’t get the message—and, most of all, someone who didn’t belong. 

In Blockers Lewis tells the story of seven people who believed they had a calling, who were convinced they were doing something the country couldn’t do without, and then discovered they were no longer wanted. One kept Americans’ most sensitive tax data out of the wrong hands, and another made sure that politicians and civil servants played by the rules. One figured out how to stop wildfires from destroying suburban neighborhoods, another helped uncover the mysteries of cystic fibrosis. 

There was also a security guard. 

It should come as no surprise that the writer who made subprime mortgages gripping (The Big Short) and turned baseball statistics into poetry (Moneyball) could transform the first two years of the second Trump administration into a thriller about federal employees. But he does. And he also puts before us a clear question: If these public servants can’t survive in government today, then what does that say about us?

event.title: Journalism for Every Writer
event.description:
Journalism isn’t only for journalists. The practice involves skills that are useful to any and all writers across genres and levels of experience. At its core, reporting is the process of asking questions and seeking answers, which is something all writers do in one form or another. In addition to interviews, research is a valuable tool for any writer to deepen and expand their understanding of a chosen subject and fact-checking can heighten the rigor and truth of any work, even the most fantastical fiction.

As part of their training, journalists learn how to distill a story down to its core components, make it legible to a wide audience, and structure information to maximize impact. These are skills and practices that all writers can benefit from. Whether there’s a journalist character in your novel, a historical component to your memoir, a narrative aspect to your academic work, or a poem that provides a glimpse into an unknown world, this class will provide a basic understanding of journalism that any writer can apply to any project.

Course outcomes:
● Writers are introduced to the fundamentals of reporting, research, writing, editing and fact-checking
● Writers explore how to incorporate these skills into their writing practice
● Writers gain confidence applying these skills in their own projects, outside of the classroom

Class schedule:
Week 1: The Journalist Mindset—Week 1 provides an overarching introduction to the key concepts of journalism and how it can be applied to any writing project. Concepts include the “5 Ws + H” and newsworthiness.

Week 2: Reporting and Research—Students will learn interview techniques; discuss other ways to access information, like court documents, public records and archives; and review best practices for research, like relying on primary source documents and vetting journal articles.

Week 3: Writing & Structure—How to write and structure a basic news story, with a discussion of how those core principles (like the inverted pyramid) can apply to any writing project. It will also address how to approach writing a feature story, which requires using information to build scenes and character development.

Week 4: Ethics & Accuracy—How to fact-check and why it matters. Students will learn what goes into fact-checking and how to ensure that the information they have gathered is accurate. They will also learn core ethical principles of journalism, such as objectivity, independence, as well as how to handle attribution (on vs off the record) and how to handle sources requesting anonymity or who are not telling the truth.

Week 5: Organization and Pitching. In this session, students will get tips on how to keep all their reporting notes and material organized to help streamline the writing, editing and fact-checking process. The class will also cover the basics and best practices of pitching so students feel empowered to send their ideas out into the world.

Week 6: Workshop. The final class will be dedicated to discussing each student’s ideas and providing collective guidance and feedback. Whether it’s a question about a story’s angle or a full-fledged pitch, this session will be a forum for everyone to take their journalistic aspirations to the next level, incorporating what they’ve learned over the past five weeks.

event.title: Theodor Adorno: Minima Moralia
event.description:
When the nation and culture you grew up in and love have been taken over by a war-waging fascist dictatorship, how do you come to understand the nature and causes of what has happened? Perhaps you can do this only after you fled for your life. How then would you look at the ruins left inside yourself? This was the situation faced by one of the most sophisticated and profound thinkers of the twentieth century, Theodor Adorno (1903–1969), when he found himself living in Los Angeles during World War II after escaping from Nazi Germany.

In this Delve we will study Adorno’s Minima Moralia: Reflections from Damaged Life—the amazing book he wrote between 1944 and 1949 to explore his feelings about the calamitous situation of a world facing despotism. We will read the entire book and focus on selected essays. The book is made up of 153 very short essays, ranging from 1-3 pages. The essays focus his philosophical genius on deeply observed and subtle aspects of ourselves that contribute to or resist the ways in which we are socialized that result in alienation, loss of will and agency, and unfulfillment. He explores consumer culture, the arts, and politics along with his recollections of the rise of fascism. Each essay is a deep and intricate knot of feelings and ideas, presented by a contemplative, perseverant, unblinking thinker of the highest order Although written in grief, Adorno always seeks hope by confronting, with maximum honesty and penetration, the deep roots of the problems human society faces. Minima Moralia is a monument to the sensitive study of culture and our psyches amidst disaster trauma. Adorno’s brilliant and strong style make this book a pleasure to think with. In this Delve we will read the entire book and focus on selected entries.

Text:
Minima Moralia: Reflections from Damaged Life<, Theodor Adorno, translator E. F. N. Jephcott (Verso)

event.title: Claire Keegan: Small Things Like These  and Foster
event.description:
In rating Small Things Like These 41st on its list of the 100 Best Books of the 21st Century, the New York Times said: “Not a word is wasted in Keegan’s small, burnished gem of a novel, a sort of Dickensian miniature….”

This is an important novella in the vein of Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, but with an ending that packs a different punch. At its center is a man torn between family, community, church, and one young woman in a terrible predicament. He must make a choice, and Keegan’s exquisite, concise writing reveals that agonizing choice. It’s a perfect story to ponder and discuss: What would you choose in his situation?

Keegan’s other work, “Foster,” is a long short story with a big impact. No word is wasted as Keegan tells the story of a young girl sent to live with another family when her own mother is fraught with problems of her own. Again, in the New York Times’s glowing review they say: “Keegan makes us complicit in what her characters want, setting us up for utter heartbreak when they don’t get it.”

Foster’s is already considered canonical and is taught as a required text for Comparative Literature in the curriculum for Ireland’s secondary schools.

Join us in this two-week exploration of these incredible short works by an Irish writer of spare prose and mmense talent.

event.title: Writing with Tarot
event.description:
Ever try doing a tarot reading for one of your characters? Writing a poem inspired by the images on a tarot card? Tarot is both deeply symbolic and highly narrative, creating a system that can inspire and guide many forms of writing. This multigenre workshop will introduce techniques for using tarot in one’s writing practice. We’ll use tarot cards to generate new ideas and new writing through writing exercises; practice character, story, and image development using tarot symbols; learn how tarot can help us plumb the depths of our ideas; and discover how to work with the tarot from generation through revision. This generative class is open to writers in any genre.

No experience with tarot is necessary prior to the first workshop. If you have your own deck, please have it handy. Links to free online decks and resources will be sent to participants prior to the first class.

Class outcomes:
• Practice using tarot for a variety of writing purposes, from generating ideas through revision.
• Explore the fundamentals of tarot through writing exercises and discussion.
• Work with tarot images, narratives, and characters from many different decks.

event.title: Rebecca Handler in conversation with Selina Fillinger
event.description:
The Literary Arts Bookstore is pleased to welcome author Rebecca Handler to celebrate her new novel, In the Round. Handler will be joined in conversation by Selina Fillinger.

About the book:

Have you ever been dead certain that you’re being observed, that maybe your very existence is predicated on how others see you? A few minutes after she’s become convinced she’s the victim of a home invasion, In the Round’s brilliant and intimate narrator plunges us into a feminist Kafkaesque literary mystery that unfolds over the course of one weird—and dare we say, dramatic—night in San Francisco. Nothing is missing from her family’s home, but everything feels wrong. So begins a sleepless night of questioning, and a novel packed with the kind of astonishing twists that leave readers wondering: Is all the world a stage, after all? Over the course of the evening, theatrical elements creep in: a cast list, a prop list, an intermission.

At once an avant-garde thriller, a meditation on motherhood and mortality, a full-throated endorsement of gut-level intuition, and a tribute to the rapture of live theater in a post-pandemic world, In the Round is a lively, inventive, and completely singular story.

event.title: The Moth Mainstage: Tightrope
event.description:
This December, The Moth’s anticipated Mainstage season comes to Portland in partnership with Literary Arts.

One foot in front of another…

Join The Moth this fall for TIGHTROPE, an evening of extraordinary true stories about what happens when there’s no clear path—only the courage to keep moving forward.

Stories of balancing without a net. Trusting your gut. Taking the leap before you know where you’ll land. Of big gambles and near misses, quiet acts of bravery and glorious mistakes. Of sending the text, booking the flight, sharing the secret you’ve carried for years, and watching everything change.

The Mainstage tour is The Moth’s signature live show, featuring a carefully curated lineup of tellers—writers, artists, adventurers, community members, and unexpected voices—sharing true personal stories, told live and without notes.

Come spend an evening on the edge. One step can change the whole story.

About The Moth

The Moth is a global storytelling nonprofit with the mission to inspire people to listen and share openly, think and feel deeply, and expand their understanding of one another. Since 1997, The Moth has presented more than 70,000 true stories—told live and without notes—in 11 countries, across 4 continents. Today, The Moth produces 600+ live shows annually, as well as the Peabody Award-winning The Moth Radio Hour, and the popular The Moth Podcast. Through workshops for students, educators, adults, advocates, and professionals, The Moth guides thousands of new storytellers each year in finding and sharing their own voices. Learn more at themoth.org

event.title: Charles Dickens: Our Mutual Friend
event.description:
Some critics of British 19th century novels place Dickens’s final completed novel, Our Mutual Friend, alongside other great novels of that era: Middlemarch, by George Eliot; Vanity Fair, by William Makepeace Thackeray; The Way We Live Now, by Anthony Trollope; and Jane Eyre, by Charlotte Bronte.

This novel is darker, more brooding, than any of those. Rather than years or decades in his past to create a feeling of nostalgia, at the end of his 40th year as a published writer and most of the time the most famous and popular writer in the English language, Dickens turns his pen onto a satiric look London’s pursuit of Money and Society, and a bitter one at the state of the poor and those whose living are derived from the great and polluted River Thames, the powerful controlling symbol that unites many of the characters and plots in the novel.

In this six-week Delve we will discuss those issues, the novel’s place in Dickens’s development as an artist, and experience a novel filled with death, deceit, riverside dives, and disguises.

Our Mutual Friend by Charles Dickens
Note the Penguin Classics edition, with notes and introduction by Adrian Poole is the preferred edition for this seminar

event.title: Yu Miri: Tokyo Ueno Station
event.description:
Kazu is dead. But that doesn’t stop him from reliving his life and his choices in a vulnerable, moving voice, through memories shaped by experience, regret, and ultimate loss.

When Yu Miri’s Tokyo Ueno Station, translated by Morgan Giles, won the 2020 National Book Award for Translated Literature, the judges described the novel as “an observation of Japan at the gateway of its capital, at multiple thresholds of shifting eras, told in the bardo of a mourning father and compatriot, reciting his surroundings and circumstances as if a prayer, a mantra.”

In this Delve Seminar, we’ll take the path suggested by the prize judges, treating the text as a model and starting point to “recite our surroundings and circumstances.” Through journaling and discussion, we’ll work our way toward a greater understanding of the novel’s view on contemporary Japan, and the fractured structure Yu employs to explore one man’s memories. Over the course of our time together, we’ll gain insights into our own places, decisions, losses, and joys, reading and journaling toward a finer understanding of life’s fragility and resilience.

This seminar will meet four times. Participants should expect 40-50 pages of reading per week and are invited to journal in response to Kazu, his choices, and the novel’s depiction of place. In addition, our discussions will be punctuated by guided reflections.

Text
Tokyo Ueno Station by Yu Miri

Reading Schedule
Week 1
Read pages 1-36. Considering fragmentation, refrain, and the weight of accumulated memories.

Week 2
Read pages 36-82. Considering grief, ritual, responsibility, expectations, and the social/cultural roles we play.

Weekn 3
Read pages 82-136. Considering landscape, history, and the personal inheritances from both; also, re-considering the fragmentation of memory.

Week 4
Read pages 136-180. Considering choice, sacrifice, confession, and how fractured memories come together to form a singular portrait.

event.title: Reimagining the Books That Shaped Us
event.description:
In this four week Delve, we’ll revisit four iconic works of middle grade fiction—Island of the Blue Dolphins, Hatchet, Julie of the Wolves, and Jacob Have I Loved. We will come to these books as adults with new questions. Part of our exploration will be the books’ covers: how they changed across decades, how marketing shaped their reception, and how visual design influenced the way young readers approached them. Throughout the course, we will weave between how the books existed in their time and what they have to offer us now.

We remember the class sets of these books or a well-used copy found in the room of an older sibling. Now, decades later, these stories can offer us something new. They become artifacts of our own reading histories that can provide comfort in stressful times, as well as teach us new things about gender and why certain books get canonized for children. If these books are new, we will also have time to discuss the books you do remember and how different educational experiences shape the titles children are exposed to in formative reading years.

Week 1: Island of the Blue Dolphins: The Complete Reader’s Edition by Scott O’Dell. Edited by Sara Schwebel. University of California Press: 2016. We will be using the annotated version of the text.

Week 2: Hatchet by Gary Paulsen. Simon & Schuster Books for Young Readers: 2006.

Week 3: Julie of the Wolves by Jean Craighead George: Harper Collins: 1997.

Week 4: Jacob Have I Loved by Katherine Paterson. Harper Collins: 1990.

event.description:
If you’re looking to become known for an idea and respected for your expertise – it’s time to write your nonfiction book.
You already have something to say. You’ve said it in rooms, in conversations, in work that has changed people. But the book? That feels like a different thing entirely – bigger, more elusive, somehow always not quite the right time.

This six-week intensive is for the writer who has lived their subject matter. The expert, the advocate, the practitioner, the person who has earned their perspective and is ready to shape it into something that lasts. Each session combines direct instruction with hands-on writing practice, guided research, breakout group work, and mastermind-style coaching — so students leave every class with something made, not just something learned. A craft thread runs through every session: every workshop produces actual writing, not just planning documents.

Who this class is for:
Nonfiction writers at any stage and any publishing path — whether you have a full draft, a half-formed concept, or simply the deep certainty that there is a book inside you. No prior publishing experience required. Especially well-suited to practitioners, educators, advocates, and entrepreneurs who want to translate their expertise into a book.

Class Schedule:

Week 1: Why this book, why you, why now.
Types of nonfiction and publishing paths overview. The identity question: who gets to write a book, and why that question is worth examining before you write a word.
Workshop: draft your three whys and write the first version of your “why you” paragraph — the one that answers why you are the only person who can write this book.

Week 2: Prove there’s a reader.
Market analysis, comp analysis, finding the gap your book fills. How to read a comp not just as a sales tool but as a craft model.
Workshop: guided research session, comp identification, group share-out. Each student writes one paragraph of market analysis for their own book.

Week 3: Build the architecture.
Book structure — chronological, topical, problem-solution. The difference between a book idea and a book argument. Finding your hook.
Workshop: draft a chapter framework and write your opening hook — the first sentence or paragraph that earns the reader’s attention.
Breakout groups workshop each other’s hooks and structures. Optional guest author perspective on structure.

Week 4: Your voice on the page.
What makes nonfiction writing compelling rather than merely informational. Voice, specificity, the role of personal story even in prescriptive work. How to write toward your reader without losing yourself.
Workshop: generative writing exercise — each student writes a scene, anecdote, or opening that demonstrates their voice. Mastermind-style coaching on what’s working and where to push further.

Week 5: Your author identity and platform.
Who you are before the book comes out matters as much as who you are after. Platform audit — what you already have, what you need, how to build now. PR angles, community strategy, the difference between an audience and a platform. Publishing paths in depth and how early decisions shape later options.
Workshop: draft your author bio. Mastermind-style coaching on individual platform gaps and publishing path decisions.

Week 6: Showcase and next steps.
Each student presents their concept to the group: their why, their reader, their structure, their hook, their voice. Structured peer feedback. Optional guest — a working author, publisher, or agent.
Every student leaves with a written concept overview, a comp list, a structural framework, a voice sample, and an author bio draft.
Students pursuing traditional publishing leave with the bones of a proposal. Students going indie leave with a positioning and launch strategy.

Goals and Outcomes:

  • A clearly defined book concept with working title and core argument
  • A comp list and market analysis paragraph
  • A chapter-by-chapter structural framework
  • A written opening hook and voice sample
  • A drafted author bio
  • A clear publishing path and next steps, whether traditional, hybrid, or independent
  • A peer community of nonfiction writers to carry the work forward

event.title: After: Poems in Conversation
event.description:
No poem is written alone. Every poem is in conversation with the writing that came before it. This conversation crosses generations and cultures, erasing distances of time, space, and mortality. In this four-part class, we’ll make that conversation intentional. We’ll consider the what, why, and how of writing in dialogue with other writers: what it means to write “after” someone, why we might quote, echo, erase, or respond to another text, and how we might do so with care, integrity, and proper credit. We’ll read poems by historical and contemporary poets who write in conversation with other poets, novelists, essayists, scientists, journalists, and historical documents. Approaches we’ll consider include: the epigraph and homage, collage and quotation, the cento, found poetry, erasure, and the response poem. In our first two classes, we’ll read examples and try generative exercises. In our second two classes, we’ll share our work and offer supportive feedback on each other’s conversations. No previous experience in writing poetry is required; all are welcome.

event.title: Reading & Looking
event.description:
Join us for a Delve seminar in which we will explore a wide range of visual art alongside short essays and books by artists, novelists, philosophers, filmmakers, and poets. Together we will read a series of classic unconventional short texts, both old and new, that examine the complex roles color (culminating with a deep dive into the color blue) plays in literature, the fine arts, philosophy, music, and daily life. We are said to be a visual culture, but few people read images as critically as text. To sharpen our seeing in both forms is what this seminar hopes to achieve, as critical reading in one deepens the experience of the other. Together we will consider such questions as: how do we “read” an image as opposed to a text and vice versa? What are the similarities and differences between verbal and visual media?

Our gateway into the world of color will be two classic essays by art critic and Booker Prize winning novelist John Berger devoted to some of the earliest artistic visions extant: the Paleolithic drawings found in Chauvet cave and the mesmerizing Fayum portraits from Greco-Roman Egypt. We will follow these pieces with two sessions on Derek Jarman’s book Chroma: A Book of Color—a genre-bending memoir that examines the color spectrum and its effect on memory in a series of insightful, playful short chapters, written as he was losing his sight at the end of his life. Eventually Jarman was able to see only in shades of blue—circumstances that make his ruminations on color both powerful and poignant. Our next session will take us into Ludwig Wittgenstein’s mind-expanding thoughts on color perception via excerpts from his Remarks on Color, which we couple with painter and writer Amy Sillman’s insights into how artists approach color—both explore their struggle with words to convey the rich spectrum of experience. The seminar culminates with two sessions on Maggie Nelson’s Bluets, an equally genre-bending experiment in autobiography—an exploration of how we see (or what we miss) and a love letter to blue as color, mood (loss, joy), and its role in art and in life.

Alongside these readings, in each session, using the large screen in Literary Arts’ seminar room, we will look at works of art (both painting and photography ranging from the very oldest work to contemporary art) that are either referred to in the texts or that can be placed in fruitful conversation with the readings. Together we will take a chromophilic journey into the realms of vision, visual pleasure, language, and literature.

Texts:
Chroma: A Book of Color by Derak Jarman
Bluets by Maggie Nelson
Excerpts from Wittgenstein and the essays by Berger and Sillman will be supplied by PDF. Participants will be sent files of the images we will be discussing prior to each session.

event.title: Writing the Novel
event.description:
Writing novels can seem like a mystical process. Write every day, and a novel will appear. The work can feel isolating and disorienting, particularly for a writer’s first book, like stumbling around in the dark. This 16-week course is designed to prepare writers for every stage of the novel writing process from beginning the first draft to finding an agent/editor once the manuscript is complete. The purpose of this course is two-fold: to discuss the novel-writing process and to create a community of writers working alongside one another. Students will leave the course well on their way to a first draft of a novel and a clear understanding of what comes next. Though this class is craft/discussion based, there will be a couple moments to share work and receive feedback from the class.

For fiction writers who are at an intermediate level and beyond.

Weeks 1 – 4: How to Begin? The first four weeks will be a look at how other writers begin their first drafts. Some writers may prefer to outline before writing the first page. Others work by discovering the story as they write it. We’ll discuss how to carve out time and create the space necessary to write a book. There’ll be lots of generative writing exercises and lots of room for discussion.

Weeks 5 – 8: Getting Across the Finish Line. Often, writers can get stuck revising and editing the first hundred pages before the first draft is ever complete. We’ll work through how to move past common creativity jams in first drafts. The goal is not to finish a perfect first draft but to finish a first draft that can be made perfect.

Weeks 9 – 12: Sculpting the Block of Marble. Once a first draft is completed, the real work begins. In this section, the focus will be on how to outline, rewrite, and revise the novel. Students will receive tools so the process can be as efficient and effective as possible.

Weeks 13 – 16: What to Expect When You’re Expecting. The last four weeks will look at what comes after completing a tight, edited novel. Topics include: incorporating notes from beta readers and editors, finding the right agent/editor for your work, and what to expect in the year up to publication.

event.title: Everybody Reads 2027: Louise Erdrich
event.description:
Literary Arts is pleased to present New York Times bestselling author Louise Erdrich at the Arlene Schnitzer Concert Hall on March 18, 2027.  

Her appearance will conclude months of engaging programs and events through Multnomah County Library’s Everybody Reads program, a community-wide project that promotes shared reading and discussion around a single book.  

Erdrich’s 2025 novel, The Mighty Red, is the library’s 2027 reading selection and the focal point of this year’s Everybody Reads. From January through March, library-led discussions and activities will center on the book’s themes around love, family, time, and the complexities of being human.  

About the book:

In this stunning novel, Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award–winning author Louise Erdrich tells a story of love, natural forces, spiritual yearnings, and the tragic impact of uncontrollable circumstances on ordinary people’s lives.

In the Red River Valley of North Dakota, several lives revolve around a wedding fraught with desire, jealousy, and uncertainty. Gary Geist, a terrified young man set to inherit two farms, is desperate to marry Kismet Poe, an impulsive, lapsed goth who can’t read her own future but will settle for fulfilling his. Her best friend, Hugo, a gentle, red-haired, homeschooled giant, also loves Kismet and is determined to steal her away and build a life together. Kismet’s mother, Crystal, drives a truck for Gary’s family, and on her nightly runs, tunes in to the darkness of late-night radio, experiences visions of guardian angels, and worries about what’s to come, for her daughter and herself.

The Mighty Red is Louise Erdrich at her consummate best. A novel of tender humor, disquietude, yearning, community, and family, it is about ordinary people who dream, grow up, fall in love, struggle, endure tragedy, carry bitter secrets; men and women both complicated and contradictory, flawed and decent, lonely and hopeful. Human time, deep time, Red River time, and geological time are explored alongside the impact of crises in our own time—climate change, the depletion of natural resources, the economic meltdown of 2008. It is a story about our tattered bond with the earth, and about love in all of its absurdity and splendor.

Free with admission

There must be at least one adult in the room at all times with each family group.

Ages 3 and under – highly encouraged.

event.title: VCU Living Lab Research Demos – Downtown
event.description:
VCU psychology students, under the guidance of Dr. Marcia Winter, conduct research demonstrations on the museum floor, sharing insights from studies done through the National Living Lab network. Later in the semester, students will also conduct a live research study on children’s pre-writing skills with families who provide consent, coordinated by Dr. Virginia Chu from VCU’s Department of Occupational Therapy.

Visitors are welcome to stop by to observe the demonstrations and learn about the research process and, if interested, participate in a one-on-one live study.

Please note: This is not a general museum activity. Participation in the live study is one-on-one and limited to one family at a time. Visitors are welcome to stop by to observe the demonstrations and learn about the research process.

Every First Friday the Lancaster Science Factory offers free admission from 5 – 7pm for the first 300 guests. Explore over 80 interactive exhibits for kids in grades K – 8 and their families! This program is possible through the generous support of PPL.

Manufacturing First Friday is sponsored by ManTec! There will be fun, hands-on, manufacturing themed activities all over the museum, including Make 717 and robotics team One Small Step for an Axolotl!

event.description:
Night Owls 

Friday October 9th, 2026, 5:00 – 8:00 PM 

Experience an evening of science and discovery after dark at the Lancaster Science Factory. 

Explore the Science Factory, enjoy special owl-themed activities, and learn all about these fascinating nocturnal animals. 

Live Owl Presentations 

Presented by Raven Ridge Wildlife Center 

Join us for a special live owl presentation featuring Horus and Khonsu. 

Showtimes: 

  • 5:30 PM 
  • 6:15 PM 
  • 7:00 PM 

Owl presentation tickets are $3 per person in addition to general admission. Lancaster Science Factory members receive 10% off the owl presentation ticket. 

Space is limited, so advance tickets are recommended. 

More Owl Activities 

Throughout the evening, enjoy additional owl-themed activities included with your admission. 

Owl Pellet Investigation
Discover what an owl has been eating by examining real owl pellets and uncovering the clues inside. 

Science Café
Get hands-on with real owl specimens and discover how wings, feet, and skulls help owls survive and thrive. 

Plus, explore all of your favorite Lancaster Science Factory exhibits throughout the evening. 

General admission is required to attend Night Owls. Owl presentation tickets are sold separately.

event.title: Archaeology Day
event.description:
Have you ever wondered how archaeologists uncover stories from prehistoric times? Do you have a mysterious artifact at home and are curious if it’s the real deal?

Meet the experts who can help unlock those answers during Pennsylvania Archaeology Month at Meadowcroft Rockshelter! Archaeologists from the Society for Pennsylvania Archaeology will be on-site to bring history to life through engaging talks, hands-on artifact identification, and live demonstrations of prehistoric tools and technology.

Whether you’re a history buff or a curious explorer, this is your chance to step into the shoes of an archaeologist and uncover the secrets of the past!

Admission

Access to Archaeology Day at Meadowcroft is included with regular admission. All kids aged 17 and under receive free admission, thanks to UPMC and UPMC Health Plan. Purchasing tickets in advance is encouraged.

event.title: Living History: The 1776 Gathering at Fort Pitt
event.description:
Discover the story of a pivotal 1776 conference that brought Continental Congress representatives and Native leaders together at Fort Pitt.

Join Fort Pitt Museum Living History Coordinator Lukas Smith and DJ Huff, a member of the Seneca Nation, as they commemorate the gathering with special living history presentations.

In October 1776, Jasper Yeates, a Pennsylvania lawyer appointed by the Continental Congress as a commissioner for Indian affairs, traveled to Fort Pitt to work alongside George Morgan, the Continental Congress’s Indian agent at Fort Pitt, and other commissioners. Together, they met with representatives of Native nations in the Ohio Country as American officials sought neutrality during the growing Revolutionary War.

Experience this moment in history with living history vignettes and musket and rifle demonstrations at 1, 2, and 3 p.m. on the Fort Pitt Museum lawn, weather permitting.

Admission

The living history vignettes and rifle demonstrations are free to attend. Regular admission applies to enter the museum and explore its exhibitions.

event.title: Walk in Penn’s Woods
event.description:
Explore Pennsylvania’s natural history on a guided woodland walk that connects the past to the present.

In partnership with the Pennsylvania Forestry Association, Penn State, the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, and other organizations across the commonwealth, Meadowcroft will host an immersive educational walk through its surrounding landscape.

Step into the footsteps of prehistoric hunter-gatherers and discover how early inhabitants relied on native plants and wildlife for food, tools, and survival. Along the way, learn how Pennsylvania’s forests have evolved over time and why they remain vital today.

Admission

Walk in Penn’s Woods is included with admission. Purchasing tickets in advance is encouraged, but tickets will also be sold at the admissions desk in the Barensfeld Center depending on availability.

event.title: Teacher Training: Surviving the Ice Age
event.description:
Ever wonder how humans survived the Ice Age? Interested in bringing this fascinating topic to your students?

Teachers are invited to join the History Center and Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village for a two-part professional development workshop that combines STEM and the humanities to uncover the story of our prehistoric ancestors.

Hosted at the History Center and Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village, this unique program explores the science of the Ice Age alongside the archaeological discoveries that continue to reshape our understanding of the first peoples of the Americas.

Part 1 on Tuesday, Oct. 6, at the Heinz History Center (5 to 8 p.m.)

Enjoy a guided tour of Planet Ice: Mysteries of the Ice Ages and hear from experts about the science behind the Ice Age, glacial landscapes, prehistoric animals, and the remarkable adaptations that allowed humans to survive in a changing world.

Part 2 on Saturday, Oct. 10, at Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village (10 a.m. to 1 p.m.)

Visit the world-famous archaeological site that transformed our understanding of the first peoples of the Americas. Tour Meadowcroft Rockshelter, explore the latest archaeological discoveries, and learn how evidence from the site connects to the stories explored in Planet Ice.

Reserve tickets

Admission

This two-day Act 48 workshop is $15 for educators with advance registration. Participation in both the Oct. 6 and Oct. 10 workshops is required.

Act 48 credits will be provided for an additional $5.

For additional questions, please contact learn@heinzhistorycenter.org.

event.title: Game Changers: Franco’s Italian Army
event.description:
During this special panel discussion kicking off Italian Heritage Month, Anne Madarasz, director of the Franco Harris Sports Museum, and Melissa E. Marinaro, director of the Italian American Program, will join original members of Franco’s Italian Army and special guests to share stories and explore the group’s lasting cultural and social impact.

The program will not only remember and celebrate Franco’s Italian Army, but also reflect on issues related to ethnicity, identity, and the enduring legacy of the 1970s.

In 1972, Steelers rookie running back Franco Harris took the NFL by storm. A first-round draft pick, Harris finished the season with 1,055 rushing yards, a Pro Bowl nomination, and an NFL Rookie of the Year Award.

His breakout season inspired a new kind of Steelers fandom. That November, a group of fans traded black and gold for the green, white, and red Italian Tricolor and marched onto the scene as Franco’s Italian Army, just as the Steelers were battling for their first division championship in 1972.

Originally made up of second-generation Italian Americans from Pittsburgh’s East Liberty neighborhood, home to one of Pittsburgh’s historic Little Italies, the Army celebrated Franco’s heritage and reinforced their own ethnic pride and traditions in their Steelers fandom by including Italian food, wine, and gear in their game day traditions.

The Franco Harris Sports Museum’s annual Game Changers program explores the people, stories, and pivotal moments in Western Pennsylvania sports history that have transformed Pittsburgh and left a lasting impact beyond the playing field.

Join Fort Pitt Museum Living History Coordinator Lukas Smith for a look at the curious locals and travelers drawn to the site of the Battle of the Monongahela.

event.title: Behind the Excavation: Stories from a Life in Archaeology
event.description:
In the 1970s,  Dr. Landers was part of the groundbreaking excavation team at Meadowcroft Rockshelter when archaeologists uncovered evidence of human habitation dating back nearly 19,000 years.

That discovery not only transformed history’s understanding of when people first arrived in North America; it marked the beginning of Dr. Lander’s remarkable 40-year career.

Join Dr. Landers in conversation with Dave Scofield, Director of Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village, as they discuss the discoveries that shaped her career and the people and places she encountered along the way.

Hear firsthand stories from her time at Meadowcroft and behind-the-scenes insights from a career spent uncovering the past.

Before the program, explore Planet Ice: Mysteries of the Ice Ages on the History Center’s first floor. The exhibit features authentic Paleoindian tools and artifacts from Meadowcroft, including an elk tooth and passenger pigeon bones recovered from the Rockshelter.

Admission

Admission is $10 for non-members and $5 for members. The program will take place in the museum’s fifth floor Mueller Center.

American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation will be available upon request. Please contact us at programs@heinzhistorycenter.org in advance to request accommodations.

About Dr. Landers

Dr. Diane Beynon Landers is a seasoned archaeologist with over 40 years of experience. A graduate of Muskingum University with an MBA from Point Park University and a Ph.D. in Anthropology from the University of Pittsburgh, she studied under Dr. James Adovasio, renowned for his work at Meadowcroft Rockshelter. Dr. Landers wrote her dissertation on Meadowcroft and later became an Associate Professor at Indiana University, where she developed the first archaeology program at the Fort Wayne campus.

Returning to Pittsburgh, she joined GAI Consultants, where she became the first female Vice President and Board Member. As a consulting archaeologist, she managed significant historic and prehistoric excavations, including projects in Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and at National Battlefields like Fort Necessity and Gettysburg.

Dr. Landers is also a native Pittsburgher with deep family ties to the city’s real estate development. She volunteers on the board of the Pittsburgh CLO and serves as Chair of the Meadowcroft Advisory Board, where she continues her work in archaeology.

event.title: Henry Koerner’s Once and Future Pittsburgh
event.description:
Image: Henry Koerner, American, 1915-1991; Oh Fearful Wonder of Man (detail), 1962, oil on canvas, 88 3/16 × 102 3/8 in. (224 × 260 cm); Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh, The Henry L. Hillman Fund, 81.68; © Henry Koerner. By permission

When Henry Koerner arrived in Pittsburgh from New York in 1952, the American art world was changing. Koerner, a Jewish refugee from Vienna, was known for his distinctive style of magical realism, which was quickly being overshadowed by the rise of abstract expressionism.

But in Pittsburgh, he found new inspiration. The city’s epic vistas, gritty characters, and unexpected encounters became rich subjects for his work, while Pittsburgh itself offered a place where his artistic practice could flourish.

To honor the 35th anniversary of Koerner’s death, the Rauh Jewish Archives will look back at his Pittsburgh career and look ahead to his enduring legacy through four unique perspectives:

  • A local art historian will explore Koerner’s career in Pittsburgh.
  • A member of Koerner’s family and fellow art historian will offer both a personal and professional perspective on his life and work.
  • A documentary filmmaker will examine Koerner’s story through the lens of film.
  • The preservationist who purchased Koerner’s iconic Squirrel Hill home will reflect on the importance of preserving his legacy for future generations.

Together, these perspectives will paint a fuller portrait of Koerner, his relationship with Pittsburgh, and the lasting impact of his work on the city.

This program is presented in partnership with Concept Art Gallery.

About the Speakers

Dr Alex Taylor is an historian of modern American art and visual culture at the University of Pittsburgh. His research strives to locate works of art within the histories of global capitalism, consumption, and mass media. His interests include transnational modernisms, studio practice, artistic self-fashioning, patrons and patronage, advertising, consumer cultures, and the intersections between artistic, political, and economic life.

Dr. Joseph Koerner is a son of Henry Koerner and chair of the Department of Art and Architecture at Harvard University, where he teaches the history of art and architecture from the late Middle Ages to the present, with a focus on Northern Renaissance art, Dutch seventeenth-century, European Romanticism, and German and Austrian Modernism.

William Murphy is the Director of Operations at the Postwar Gallery in Homewood and the editor of several documentary projects about Koerner and his work.

Caroline Boyce is a preservationist and curator. Since purchasing the Koerner House in Squirrel Hill in 2021, she has worked to preserve Koerner’s artistic legacy in Pittsburgh and abroad.

About the Speakers

Hollen Barmer and Miranda Crotsley are the co-founders of Land and Kin Collaborative, a business dedicated to history and genealogy for people and places. They have been working together on house histories and family tree mysteries since 2014, serving clients around Western Pennsylvania and the United States. Since 2022, they have presented public workshops and conducted consulting sessions on investigating house histories. In addition, they collaborate with partners to uncover, research, and present local history topics ranging from enslavement in 18th and 19th century Pittsburgh to mysterious explosions and sensational trials of the 1920s.

When they are not digging into the history of old houses or telling neighborhood stories, they work in fields that involve storytelling, investigation, and history. Miranda Crotsley is an educator and Program Coordinator in PA State Parks at Jennings Environmental Education Center where she researches and develops programming around park natural and cultural history including a reconstructed 1820s-era tavern inn, an original 19th century one-room schoolhouse, and a 20th century abandoned coal mine. Hollen Barmer is a strategic communications manager, working with technical researchers to tell the stories of their work.

event.title: A Keystone Story: Pennsylvania’s Negro League Legacy
event.description:
Join the Josh Gibson Foundation for its annual Negro League Baseball Symposium, “A Keystone Story: Pennsylvania’s Negro League Legacy,” hosted in partnership with the Franco Harris Sports Museum at the History Center.

The program will feature an all-star panel of baseball historians, including author Courtney Michelle Smith, Ph.D.; Rob Ruck, historian at the University of Pittsburgh; and Ted Knorr, founder of the Society for American Baseball Research’s Negro League Research Conference.

Ruck, a noted author who wrote “Sandlot Seasons: Sport in Black Pittsburgh,” will examine Pittsburgh’s outsized contributions to the Negro Leagues, including the legendary Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords.

Knorr, a longtime Harrisburg-based baseball researcher who has spent more than 40 years studying and preserving the history of Negro League baseball in Central Pennsylvania, will explore the history of the Harrisburg Giants. The Giants’ star-studded roster included legends like Rap Dixon, Fats Jenkins, and Spottswood Poles, whose nicknames were only surpassed by their on-field play.

Dr. Smith, a Philadelphia-based historian, professor, and author of “Jackie Robinson: A Life in American History” will share the lively history of the Philadelphia area’s Negro League teams, including the compelling story of Ed Bolden, who ran the Hilldale Club and the Philadelphia Stars during the course of his 40-year career.

Admission

This program is free with advance registration. Tickets include access to the Franco Harris Sports Museum, which features a long-term exhibition on the history of Negro League baseball in Western Pa.

American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation will be available upon request. Please contact us at programs@heinzhistorycenter.org in advance to request accommodations.

This program is presented in partnership with America250PA, established by the Pennsylvania state legislature and Governor to plan, encourage, develop and coordinate the commemoration of the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States, Pennsylvania’s integral role in that event, and the impact of its people on the nation’s past, present, and future.

Josh Gibson Foundation
The Josh Gibson Foundation believes in the endless possibilities for potential in today’s youth. By providing academic and athletic programs that foster leadership and scholarship, the skills necessary for tomorrow’s successes are created today. Its goal is to carry on the legacy of greatness and accomplishment embodied by Josh Gibson, by developing programs that help children of every level of ability reach their potential, and to create opportunities that set The Josh Gibson Foundation apart from other organizations and provides value for our communities. Learn more at joshgibson.org.

About the Speakers

Courtney Michelle Smith, Ph.D., is a historian, published author, and an avid baseball fan. Her love of baseball began in her childhood when she watched Phillies games narrated by Harry Kalas. She has retained her love for the Phillies, through all the highs and lows, and learned that she could combine her love of baseball and local history while taking a college course on Baseball & the American Tradition. That course came around the time of the 50th anniversary of Jackie Robinson’s debut with the Brooklyn Dodgers and introduced her to the history of Negro League Baseball. Her research focus on Ed Bolden, the Philadelphia Stars, and Black baseball in the Philadelphia area began over twenty years ago and led to the publication of her first book. She earned her B.A. in History and Political Science at Cabrini College and her M.A. and Ph.D. in American History Lehigh University. She lives in Delaware County, PA with her family.

Ted Knorr is a longtime Harrisburg‑based baseball researcher who has spent more than forty years studying and preserving the history of Negro League baseball in Central Pennsylvania. A retired Pennsylvania state administrator, he has devoted his post‑career life to documenting overlooked players, recovering lost box scores, and helping families and communities reconnect with their baseball heritage. Knorr founded Negro League Nights in Harrisburg, Lancaster, and York, as well as the Society for American Baseball Research’s Negro League Research Conference, now known as the Jerry Malloy Negro League Conference. His writing has appeared in SABR publications, local game programs, and newspapers, and, currently, in the online Truth Seekers Journal. He is best known for his extensive scholarship on Rap Dixon, the Georgia‑born, Steelton‑raised outfielder he has championed as a deserving Hall of Fame candidate. For the Josh Gibson Foundation’s Pennsylvania Negro League seminar, Knorr represents Harrisburg with a perspective shaped by local memory, regional pride, and decades of hands‑on research.

Rob Ruck is an historian at the University of Pittsburgh, where he teaches and writes about sport. He focuses on how people use sport to tell a collective story about who they are—to themselves and to the world.

His books include “Sandlot Seasons: Sport in Black Pittsburgh” (1987), “The Tropic of Baseball: Baseball in the Dominican Republic” (1991), “Rooney: A Sporting Life” (2010) which he wrote with his late wife, Maggie Jones Patterson, “Raceball: How the Major Leagues Colonized the Black and Latin Game” (2011), and “Tropic of Football: The Long and Perilous Journey of Samoans to the NFL” (2018). His most recent, co-authored books are “Pittsburgh Rising: From Frontier Town to Steel City” with Ted Muller and “Mal Goode Reporting: The Life and Work of a Black Broadcast Trailblazer,” with Liann Tsoukas.

His documentaries, “Kings on the Hill: Baseball’s Forgotten Men” (NBC 1995) and “The Republic of Baseball: Dominican Giants of the American Game” (2006) appeared on PBS. A member of the 2006 Hall of Fame special election committee for black and Latin players, he collaborated with the Hall of Fame on a permanent exhibit about Latinos in baseball – Viva Beisbol! – as well as Souls of The Game: The Voices of Black Baseball, which opened in Cooperstown in 2024.

America250PA and Lecture250

This program is part of the History Center’s year-long commemoration of the U.S. Semiquincentennial, marking the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, in partnership with America250PA.

The Lecture250 Series, hosted at partner locations across the Commonwealth in 2026, examines the forces that shaped Pennsylvania’s role in the American story—from the founding ideals of independence and equality to the development of industry, culture, community identity, and global connections. Each event will include a public discussion following the lecture to deepen civic engagement and invite community reflection.

Heinz History Center programs commemorating America’s 250th anniversary are supported by Nimick Forbesway Foundation, Richard King Mellon Foundation, Visit PA, and the Allegheny Regional Asset District (RAD).
